title: Smoky Mountains road named among 14 most haunted in the world
excerpt: Sixt Magazine ranked Roring Fork Motor Trail one of the most haunted in the U.S. Legends says it is haunted by the ghost of Lucy, who died in a fire.
content:
Oct. 28, 2026, 1:44 p.m. ET

  • Roaring Fork Motor Trail in Gatlinburg was named the 14th most haunted road in the world by Sixt Magazine.
  • The road is known for the legend of a ghost named Lucy, who is said to have died in a cabin fire in the early 1900s.
  • Drivers and visitors to the Great Smoky Mountains still report seeing the ghostly figure of Lucy along the trail.

A number of Great Smoky Mountains urban legends and myths have been corroborated over the years.

Many Knoxvillians have claimed to have spotted the mysterious Wampus Cat or visited the ghostly Bijou Theatre. If you're looking for another eerie Appalachian spot, look no further than Roaring Fork Motor Trail.

Roaring Fork Motor Trail, a one-way, 5.5-mile drive in Gatlinburg, was named the No. 14 most haunted road in the world by Sixt Magazine.

The roads that made the list "are places where history, mystery, and chilling folklore come together to create spine-tingling experiences for travelers brave enough to explore them," Sixt said. Roaring Fork Motor Trail is known for a creepy story that might leave drivers wondering if the hitchhiker they spotted was real or a spirit.

Roaring Fork Motor Trail known for ghost of Lucy

"Roaring Fork Motor Nature Trail in the Great Smoky Mountains near Gatlinburg is a scenic drive with a spooky side," according to Sixt.

That spooky side is a hitchhiker named Lucy.

The legend of Lucy differs slightly among accounts, but most versions of the story begin in the early 1900s, when a cabin along Roaring Fork Motor Trail caught fire.

Lucy was a member of the family that lived in the cabin, but unlike the rest of the family, she was unable to escape the flames that night and died.

This is where the pieces of the story begin to jumble and the timeline becomes muddled.

Some say the next events were 30 years later. Some say it was just two weeks, some even say it was the very next day, but all agree a man named Foster offered Lucy a ride home on his horse when he saw the young woman standing alone, cold and barefoot along Roaring Fork Motor Trail.

Some say what happened next occurred 30 years later. Others say it was just two weeks later, while some even say it was the very next day. But all agree that a man named Foster offered Lucy a ride home on his horse when he saw the young woman standing alone, cold and barefoot, along Roaring Fork Motor Trail.

Foster fell in love with Lucy. Sometime after he dropped her off, he returned to ask for her parents' permission to marry her, but Lucy's parents told Foster that she had been dead for some time.

More than a century later, people still claim to see Lucy looking for a ride near the spot where her family's cabin burned down.
